##### Binomial Distribution {#sec-eda-binomial-distribution}

**Probability Mass Function**

The binomial distribution is used when there are exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes of a trial. These outcomes are appropriately labeled "success" and "failure". The binomial distribution is used to obtain the probability of observing $x$ successes in $N$ trials, with the probability of success on a single trial denoted by $p$. The binomial distribution assumes that $p$ is fixed for all trials.

The formula for the binomial probability mass function is

$$P(x;p,n) = \binom{n}{x} (p)^{x}(1-p)^{(n-x)} \;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n$$

where

$$\binom{n}{x} = \frac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}$$

The binomial distribution is discrete, defined only at the integers $x = 0, 1, \ldots, n$, so the plots below use `geom_col()` rather than a connected line to avoid implying that the probability mass exists between integers.

The following is the plot of the binomial probability mass function for $n = 100$ and 4 different values of $p$: 0.1, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-binomial-dist-pmf
#| fig-cap: "Binomial probability mass function for four values of p (n = 100)"
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

ps <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75)

crossing(x = 0:100, p = ps) |>
  mutate(
    y = dbinom(x, size = 100, prob = p),
    p_label = paste("p =", p),
    p_label = fct_reorder(p_label, p)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~p_label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "P(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

**Cumulative Distribution Function**

The formula for the binomial cumulative probability function is

$$F(x;p,n) = \sum_{i=0}^{x}{\binom{n}{i}(p)^{i}(1-p)^{(n-i)}}$$

Because the binomial distribution is discrete, its cumulative distribution function is a right-continuous step function, so the plot below uses `geom_step()`.

The following is the plot of the binomial cumulative distribution function for the same values of $n$ and $p$ as the pmf plot above.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-binomial-dist-cdf
#| fig-cap: "Binomial cumulative distribution function for four values of p (n = 100)"
crossing(x = 0:100, p = ps) |>
  mutate(
    y = pbinom(x, size = 100, prob = p),
    p_label = paste("p =", p),
    p_label = fct_reorder(p_label, p)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_step() +
  facet_wrap(~p_label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "F(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

**Percent Point Function**

The binomial percent point function does not exist in simple closed form. It is computed numerically. Note that because this is a discrete distribution that is only defined for integer values of $x$, the percent point function is not smooth in the way the percent point function typically is for a continuous distribution.

The following is the plot of the binomial percent point function for the same values of $n$ and $p$ as the pmf plot above.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-binomial-dist-ppf
#| fig-cap: "Binomial percent point function for four values of p (n = 100)"
crossing(alpha = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 401), p = ps) |>
  mutate(
    x = qbinom(alpha, size = 100, prob = p),
    p_label = paste("p =", p),
    p_label = fct_reorder(p_label, p)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(alpha, x)) +
  geom_step() +
  facet_wrap(~p_label, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = expression(alpha), y = expression(G(alpha))) +
  theme_light()
```

**Common Statistics**

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $np$ |
| Mode | $p(n+1) - 1 \le x \le p(n+1)$ |
| Range | 0 to $n$ |
| Standard Deviation | $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\sqrt{\dfrac{(1-p)}{np}}$ |
| Skewness | $\dfrac{(1-2p)}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}$ |
| Kurtosis | $3 - \dfrac{6}{n} + \dfrac{1}{np(1-p)}$ |

**Comments**

The binomial distribution is probably the most commonly used discrete distribution.

**Parameter Estimation**

The maximum likelihood estimator of $p$ (for fixed $n$) is

$$\tilde{p} = \frac{x}{n}$$

**Software**

Most general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the binomial distribution.
